$comment: The deploy contract. deploy-api reads this instead of guessing your stack.
Making it explicit is what lets one skill deploy a Go binary and a Django app
without knowing anything about either. It also forces the migration rollback
path to be declared rather than assumed — that is the one thing an agent
genuinely cannot infer from your repository, and the thing you need most at
the exact moment you are least able to work it out.
Copy to deploy.manifest.json in the repo root and fill in.

build.$comment: Base images must be digest-pinned inside the Dockerfile too; check-invariants.sh only sees compose.

$comment_port: Container-internal only. Nothing is published to the host — cloudflared reaches this over a user-defined network by service name.

$comment: Must not depend on the database being WRITABLE. A health check that writes
turns a read-only replica or a full disk into a failed deploy and an
automatic rollback, which is the opposite of useful during an incident.
Checking the process is up and can read is the right altitude.

readiness.$comment: How to tell 'the process started' from 'it is serving'. Deploying on the first signal races the second and produces phantom failures.

$comment_down: The down path is the deliverable, not a formality. If a migration genuinely
cannot be reversed — a dropped column, a destructive backfill — set
irreversible to true and say why in irreversible_reason. deploy-api then
refuses to proceed without a fresh verified backup, because the restore
IS the rollback at that point.
Prefer expand-contract for anything destructive: add the new column, backfill,
switch reads, deploy, and only drop the old column in a later release once
the previous version is no longer running. Each step is individually
reversible, which is what makes the sequence safe.

rollback.$comment: Redeploy the previously running image digest. deploy-api records it before each deploy; without that record there is nothing to roll back TO.
